questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the subtractive logic that defines carving in stone.
questions.stem: An engineer's brief for a hard limestone cornice asks how the block will be shaped. Which statement correctly describes the process?

options.text: The carver removes stone from a solid block until the intended profile appears.
The carver builds the profile from applied layers of material over a hidden core.
options.misconception: confuses subtractive carving with additive modelling

options.text: The carver joins several carved fragments with concealed dowels to form the cornice.
options.misconception: assumes the finished form is assembled from separate pieces

options.text: The carver pours liquid stone into a mould and removes the mould once it cools.
options.misconception: confuses carving with the foundry process of casting

questions.explanation: Carving is subtractive: material is removed until the intended form is exposed. The distractors describe modelling, joinery and casting, none of which uses a chisel on solid stone.
questions.hint: Ask whether material is added or taken away.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why roughing precedes finishing in a direct carving sequence.

stimulus.body: The yard log for the north elevation records that each limestone block was marked out with ink, roughed down with a claw chisel, and only then handed to the finishing chisels.

questions.stem: Given the yard log above, which option best explains why the claw chisel was used before the finishing chisels?

options.text: The claw chisel melts the stone slightly so the finishing tools will not slip on it.
options.misconception: treats stone as a material that softens under heat

options.text: The claw chisel clears waste quickly and leaves an even bed the finishing tools need.
The claw chisel sets the ink guide lines so the finishing chisel follows them exactly.
options.misconception: believes the roughing tool only marks the layout

options.text: The claw chisel hardens the outer skin so that later chisels will not chip it.
options.misconception: invents a hardening effect that stone tools cannot produce

questions.explanation: The claw chisel clears waste quickly and leaves an even bed the finishing tools need. Melting, inking and hardening are not functions of this tool.
questions.hint: Think about what the finishing tools require first.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the freedoms and constraints of carving from a living outcrop.
questions.stem: A quarry brief requires a standing figure carved directly from the living rock of an outcrop. Explain what the method permits and what it forbids.

answer.exemplar: Carving from the living rock means the block can never be separated or reduced, so the design must be planned to fit the stone exactly as it lies in the ground. The sculptor is bound by existing cracks, bedding planes and the natural profile of the outcrop, and any error in the original layout cannot be patched by adding material later.

questions.explanation: Working from the living rock fixes the figure to its bed and removes the option of transport or rearrangement. Existing flaws and the natural profile dictate the design, so the plan must be drawn around the stone.
questions.hint: Think about what cannot be moved or added later.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Compute the mass of an alloy component needed for a specified bronze.
questions.stem: A foundry brief specifies a bronze alloy that must be 12 percent tin by mass to meet its hardness requirement. How many kilograms of tin are needed for a 25 kilogram batch?
questions.explanation: Twelve percent of 25 kilograms is 3 kilograms, and the remaining 22 kilograms would be copper. Reading the percentage as an amount of copper would give a figure the brief cannot accept.
questions.hint: Multiply the batch mass by the tin percentage.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret condition readings to decide whether a bronze can remain on display.
questions.stem: A survey of the bronze door records surface readings of 4.2 for as-cast finish, 5.8 for light dulling, 7.1 for a stable patina and 9.6 for active powdering on a 1 to 10 scale. Which reading means the door must come off display?

options.text: 5.8, because light dulling is the first sign that the alloy is chemically unstable
options.misconception: confuses harmless dulling with active corrosion

options.text: 4.2, because an as-cast finish means the surface has never been examined
options.misconception: treats an unread surface as the emergency case

options.text: 9.6, because active powdering means the corrosion is still spreading and losing metal
7.1, because a stable patina proves that moisture is trapped under the surface
options.misconception: reads a stable patina as evidence of hidden wetness

questions.explanation: A reading of 9.6 for active powdering indicates corrosion that is still advancing, so continued metal loss makes display unsafe. The other readings describe a sound surface, harmless dulling, or a patina that has stabilised.
questions.hint: Look for the reading that names an unstable surface.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Apply a percentage increase to a measured panel width.
questions.stem: First, a conservator measures the panel at 62 centimetres wide in a dry gallery. Second, the panel is moved to a damp store and its width increases by 1.2 percent. Which calculation gives the new width?

options.text: 62 divided by 1.012, giving 61.26 centimetres
options.misconception: divides by the growth factor instead of multiplying

options.text: 62 multiplied by 0.012, giving 0.744 centimetres
options.misconception: treats the percentage as the whole new width

options.text: 62 increased by 1.2, giving 63.2 centimetres
options.misconception: adds the percentage as if it were centimetres

options.text: 62 multiplied by 1.012, giving 62.744 centimetres

questions.explanation: A percentage increase means the new value is the original times one plus the rate, so 62 times 1.012 gives 62.744 centimetres. Dividing, adding the raw number, or reading the percentage as a total all misstate the movement.
questions.hint: Growth means original times one plus the rate.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The chalk ground on a panel
questions.learningObjective: Explain the function of the chalk ground beneath a panel painting.
questions.stem: In a conservation brief, a wooden panel is described as having a chalk ground applied before painting. What does that ground actually do?

options.text: It seals the wood completely so moisture can never reach the timber from the painted side.
options.misconception: believes the ground is a waterproof barrier against the wood

options.text: It provides a bright, even, absorbent surface so paint sits on the panel rather than sinking.
It adds structural thickness so the panel can carry heavier pigments without cracking.
options.misconception: confuses the preparatory layer with a reinforcement

options.text: It records the drawing of the composition so the painter need not transfer a cartoon.
options.misconception: mistakes the ground for a substitute for the cartoon

questions.explanation: The chalk ground gives a bright, uniform, absorbent surface so paint stays a layer instead of sinking into the wood. It does not seal the timber, add depth or replace the transferred drawing.
questions.hint: Think about how paint behaves on bare wood.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the tool used first when roughing hard stone.

stimulus.body: The mason's kit for the terrace job holds a point chisel, a claw chisel, a tooth chisel and a flat chisel, each with its own bevelled edge and its own rake of cut.

questions.stem: Reading the tool list above, which chisel would the mason reach for first when knocking waste off a rough block?

options.text: The claw chisel, because it grips the stone and would split the block apart
options.misconception: confuses a splitting tool with a carving tool

options.text: The tooth chisel, because its serrated edge bites hardest into the hardest stone
options.misconception: believes the serrated edge is the logical first tool

options.text: The point chisel, because it concentrates a heavy blow on a single narrow edge
The flat chisel, because a flat blade spreads the blow evenly over the whole face
options.misconception: confuses roughing out with the finishing stage

questions.explanation: The point chisel concentrates force on a narrow edge and is the standard tool for roughing hard stone before any shaping. A toothed or flat blade needs a stable surface first, and splitting is a different operation.
questions.hint: Which tool concentrates the blow on one point?

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a sculptor works directly in the block without a model.
questions.stem: A client asks the sculptor to carve a figure directly in the stone without first modelling a small version. Explain what the sculptor gains and what he or she must give up.

answer.exemplar: Working directly in the block lets the sculptor follow the stone as it is revealed, so the form can carry the tool marks and weight of the original material rather than a translation from clay. The price is that decisions cannot be undone cheaply: any mistake has to be resolved by further carving, and the whole plan must be held in the mind rather than consulted in a maquette.

questions.explanation: Direct carving lets the sculptor read the block as it is uncovered and keep the marks of the tool, but it removes the chance to test the design safely. Errors can only be resolved by carving away more material.
questions.hint: Consider reversibility of decisions made in the block.

questions.learningObjective: Read casting records to identify which stage of the bronze process failed.
questions.stem: A foundry log records three attempts: attempt one lost its wax shell in the boil, attempt two cracked the mould during burnout, attempt three poured cleanly but trapped a bubble in the largest mass. Which stage accounts for the bubble in attempt three?

options.text: The burnout stage, because the wax vapour left no channel for the metal to fill
options.misconception: attaches a bubble to an incomplete burnout

options.text: The model making stage, because the wax pattern was carved with a closed air bubble
options.misconception: blames the sculptor for a foundry defect

options.text: The mould making stage, because the plaster shell was mixed too densely to vent
options.misconception: confuses shell permeability with gas porosity

options.text: The pouring and solidifying stage, when trapped gas was held inside the cooling metal

questions.explanation: A bubble held in the casting can only form while the metal is pouring and cooling, when gas cannot escape the solidifying bronze. Earlier stages produce shells that crack or pour short, not bubbles in sound metal.
questions.hint: Which stage is the last one the metal passes through?

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Select the correct cleaning step for a stable bronze patina.
questions.stem: First, the conservator records a hard, dark green patina with no powdering and no bright metal showing. Second, she must decide whether to clean the surface. Which decision is best supported by the record?

options.text: Polish it back to bare metal, so the object shows the alloy the founder used
options.misconception: assumes a bright surface is the safest option

options.text: Leave the patina alone, because a stable adherent layer protects the metal beneath
Strip it with an aggressive solvent, because any coating hides later examination
options.misconception: treats removal of the protective layer as routine

options.text: Wash it weekly, so that new corrosion is washed away as it forms
options.misconception: believes regular washing stops stable corrosion

questions.explanation: A hard, dark green patina with no powdering is stable and adherent, and such a layer slows further corrosion, so cleaning would remove protection for no gain. Polishing or stripping exposes fresh metal, and washing does not arrest a stable surface.
questions.hint: Ask whether the patina is still moving.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify why a fitted panel splits along its grain.
questions.stem: A joinery brief notes that the wooden panel of an altarpiece is fitted into a rigid frame. Why does the panel eventually split along its grain?

options.text: Because the panel is thinner than the frame members and so carries less weight
options.misconception: confuses thickness with the cause of splitting

options.text: Because the paint layer expands faster than the wood and drags the panel apart
options.misconception: blames the paint film for a timber movement failure

options.text: Because the timber swells and shrinks with humidity while the rigid frame prevents it moving
Because the chalk ground is softer than the wood and cannot hold the surface
options.misconception: blames the preparatory layer for a structural failure

questions.explanation: Wood changes dimension as it gains and loses moisture, and a rigid frame denies it that movement, so tension opens splits along the grain. Thickness, paint and ground affect stability but do not cause the split.
questions.hint: What does the frame prevent the timber from doing?

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a mould is left to stand before metal is poured into it.

stimulus.body: The founder notes that the mould for the second attempt was set to stand for nine days after the burnout before the metal was poured, so that the shell could cool and the wax residue could be fully driven off.

questions.stem: According to the founder's record above, why must the mould stand for nine days before pouring?

options.text: To make the plaster shell brittle so that it breaks away cleanly from the casting
options.misconception: claims cooling makes plaster more brittle

options.text: To give the wax model time to harden further before the shell is broken away
options.misconception: thinks the wax model is still in place during the wait

options.text: To allow the metal to cool slowly inside the mould before it is poured out
options.misconception: reverses the order of pouring and cooling

options.text: To let the hot shell cool and clear of wax vapour before molten metal enters it

questions.explanation: A mould that is still hot and still holding wax vapour will contaminate the metal and can blow out under the pour, so it must cool and clear first. The wax model is long gone by this stage, and the pour happens before any cooling.
questions.hint: Think about what the empty shell still contains.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why panel thickness affects the severity of cracking.
questions.stem: A conservator compares two oak panels of equal width, one 8 millimetres thick and one 24 millimetres thick, both held in rigid frames in the same gallery. Explain why the thinner panel is usually in worse condition.

answer.exemplar: The two panels experience the same swings in humidity, but the thin panel moves further in any direction because it offers less material along the path of that movement. A narrow strip of wood changes dimension more than a wide slab for the same moisture content, so the thicker panel is restrained more gently and stores less stress. The thin panel therefore develops the deeper and more frequent splits along the grain.

questions.explanation: A thin panel changes dimension more for the same change in moisture, so the rigid frame restrains it harder and stores more stress. The thicker panel moves less and so splits less often and less deeply.
questions.hint: Compare how far each panel moves for the same moisture.

questions.stem: A brief sets aside 35 studio hours for carving, of which 14 hours go to roughing out the block and the remainder to finishing the form. What percentage of the hours is spent finishing?

questions.topic: The chalk ground on a panel
questions.learningObjective: Compare test panels to identify the best chalk ground recipe.
questions.stem: Four trial panels are reported: A holds paint with sharp edges on an even surface, B holds paint but the surface has gone patchy, C lets the paint sink in and the grain shows through, D has cracked along the grain. Which panel used the best ground?

options.text: Panel B, because a patchy surface shows the ground took the sizing unevenly
options.misconception: reads patchiness as evidence of a good ground

options.text: Panel A, because it both absorbed the binder and kept the paint on the surface
Panel C, because sinking paint means the ground was thin but well bonded
options.misconception: treats sinking paint as a sign of a sound ground

options.text: Panel D, because cracks along the grain prove the ground resisted panel movement
options.misconception: reads cracking as a deliberate design choice

questions.explanation: A good ground absorbs and anchors the binder while still holding the paint layer on the surface, which is what panel A shows. Sinking, patchiness and cracking each mark a fault in the ground or the panel beneath it.
questions.hint: Look for the panel where the paint stayed on top.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Choose a tool sequence that matches the state of the carved surface.
questions.stem: First, the sculptor judges the block, which still carries its sawn face. Second, the carver must choose what to do next. Which choice best fits this stage?

options.text: Draw the full design on the block with ink so no further setting out is needed
options.misconception: believes drawing replaces carving at the rough stage

options.text: Polish the surface with a flat chisel so the stone can be assessed in the light
options.misconception: starts with finishing on a surface still full of waste

options.text: Rough the block with a point chisel so the form can be read before any surface is finished
Score the block with a tooth chisel to prepare a ground for the final polish
options.misconception: treats scoring as preparation for polish

questions.explanation: A sawn block still carries all its waste, so the first job is to clear it enough for the sculptor to read the form, which is what a point chisel does. Polishing, inking and scoring all presuppose a surface already roughed down.
questions.hint: Think about what stage the surface is actually at.

questions.learningObjective: State the defining constraint of working from an unquarried outcrop.
questions.stem: A brief specifies that the sculpture will never leave the quarry. Which statement describes the defining constraint this places on the sculptor?

options.text: The sculpture must be shallow, because a deep cut would be impossible to carve in situ
options.misconception: assumes depth of cut is the limiting factor

options.text: The figure may be moved in sections once carved, so the design can be adjusted after transport
options.misconception: assumes the finished figure can still be reassembled

options.text: The stone must be polished to a mirror finish before carving, since it cannot be moved
options.misconception: invents a finishing requirement from the immobility

options.text: The design must be solved in the stone where it lies, since it cannot be moved or reassembled

questions.explanation: Once the figure is carved where it lies, it cannot be lifted, moved or pieced together again, so every decision must work with the stone in place. Nothing about depth of cut or polish follows from that.
questions.hint: Ask what cannot happen to the finished figure.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Use weight records to calculate the waste removed in carving.

stimulus.body: After the roughing week the carver weighs the block at 1,480 kilograms. When the profile is finished, the same block weighs 1,196 kilograms, and the offcuts are chipped and re-weighed at 271 kilograms.

questions.stem: Using the weighings above, what can the carver conclude about the finished block?

options.text: About 271 kilograms of waste was removed, because the chipping loss is the whole difference
options.misconception: takes the offcut weight as the full loss

options.text: About 284 kilograms of stone was removed in waste, most of it carried away during roughing
Nothing was removed, because the offcuts came from a separate stone
options.misconception: ignores the weight change between weighings

options.text: About 555 kilograms was removed, because the loss and the offcuts must both be added
options.misconception: double counts the loss and the offcuts together

questions.explanation: The block lost 1,480 minus 1,196, which is 284 kilograms, and the 271 kilograms of chips confirms that most of that loss went into waste. Adding the offcuts to the loss would count the same stone twice.
questions.hint: Compare the two block weighings before adding chips.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why harder stone is chosen for exposed architectural carving.
questions.stem: A mason asks why the cornice at the top of a north-facing stair is specified in a hard, fine-grained stone while the plinth below is in a softer, coarser one. Explain the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: The cornice is the part of the stair that carries rain, frost and hand contact, and it is also the profile that must keep its edges crisp over centuries. A hard, fine-grained stone resists weathering and holds a sharp arris, so the profile survives. The plinth sits lower, is sheltered, and only needs to bear weight, so a softer and cheaper stone is acceptable there.

questions.explanation: The exposed cornice takes the weather and must hold a crisp profile, so hard fine stone is specified for its durability. The sheltered plinth only bears load, so a softer coarse stone is acceptable there.
questions.hint: Compare the exposure and the required edge.

questions.learningObjective: Compare tool marks to identify the tools that produced them.
questions.stem: Two carvings are compared. The first shows long parallel channels scalloped at one end. The second shows overlapping shallow dishes with no directional grain. Which pair of tools most likely produced them?

options.misconception: confuses a narrow point with a wide flat cut

options.text: A flat chisel for the first and a point chisel for the second
options.misconception: reverses the tool order from the evidence

A tooth chisel for the first and a claw chisel for the second

questions.learningObjective: Convert a carving loss into a percentage of the original block.
questions.stem: First the block is weighed at 900 kilograms before any carving. Second the finished carving is weighed at 720 kilograms. What percentage of the original mass was removed?

options.text: 12 percent, because the loss of 180 is 12 percent of 1,500 kilograms
options.misconception: invents a total weight to divide the loss by

options.text: 25 percent, because 180 divided by 720 gives one quarter
options.misconception: divides the loss by the final mass instead

options.text: 80 percent, because 720 divided by 900 gives the percentage removed
options.misconception: mistakes the retained share for the removed share

options.text: 20 percent, because 180 divided by 900 gives one fifth

questions.explanation: The block lost 180 kilograms, and 180 out of the original 900 is exactly one fifth, which is 20 percent. Dividing by the finished weight, or reading the retained fraction as the removed one, inverts the calculation.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the defining advantage of the lost-wax casting process.
questions.stem: A brief asks why the bronze figure cannot be cast directly from a wooden model. Which statement gives the reason?

options.text: The wax is carved into the final shape, so the bronze simply copies the wooden model's surface
options.misconception: thinks the wax survives inside the metal

options.text: The wax is burned out of the mould, so the metal is cast into the space the wax left
The wax hardens the plaster so the mould cannot crack during the pour

options.text: The wax is replaced by sand, so the mould can be broken away and reused many times
options.misconception: confuses the wax process with sand casting

questions.learningObjective: Read a sounding test to judge how much metal survives on a bronze.

stimulus.body: After cleaning, the conservator notes that the bronze panel shows a thin dark brown layer under the green patina, and where a thumbnail was pressed the metal beneath still gives a slight metallic ring.

questions.stem: Given the condition note above, what does the slight metallic ring tell the conservator about the panel?

options.text: That the bronze has been alloyed with tin beneath the surface by the corrosion
options.misconception: claims corrosion can alloy the buried metal

options.text: That the whole panel has become a brittle corrosion product with no metal left
options.misconception: reads the ring as a sign that no metal survives

options.text: That sound metal survives beneath the corroded surface, so the loss is limited to outer layers
That the patina is hollow and will detach from the panel in sheets
options.misconception: treats the ring as evidence of delamination

questions.explanation: A metallic ring under the cleaned surface shows that sound bronze is still present beneath the corrosion, so the loss is confined to the outer layers. No alloying or hollow delamination is involved in reading that sound.
questions.hint: A ringing sound means metal is still there.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a wax model suits a complex bronze with revisions.
questions.stem: A foundry brief requires a complex bronze figure with undercut drapery and a face that must be revised three times before casting. Explain why working in wax suits this commission.

answer.exemplar: Wax is soft enough to be cut, built up and reworked with heated tools, so the sculptor can revise the drapery and the face as often as needed before anything is committed. It also burns out cleanly, leaving a cavity that reproduces fine undercut detail that a rigid mould could not release from. The metal is therefore poured into a shape the sculptor has already approved.

questions.explanation: Wax can be added, cut and reheated, so the design can be revised safely before any metal is poured, and it holds undercut detail when it burns out. A model that cannot be revised would freeze every decision before it could be tested.
questions.hint: Think about how easily wax can be changed.

questions.learningObjective: Read humidity records to explain when panel cracking is likely.
questions.stem: A gallery log records relative humidity at 45 percent for a month, then 70 percent for a week, then 50 percent for a month. When is the panel most likely to split?

options.misconception: believes weekly change cannot move timber

options.text: During the return to 50 percent, when the shrinking timber is forced by the frame
options.misconception: puts the risk at the drying stage instead

options.text: During the steady month at 45 percent, when the timber is weakest at low humidity
options.misconception: confuses slow seasonal change with sudden movement

options.text: During the week at 70 percent, when the timber swells against the rigid frame

questions.explanation: The sharpest risk comes at the jump to 70 percent, because a rapid rise in moisture swells the panel and the rigid frame resists it. A slow return to 50 percent shrinks the timber less violently, and the steady month is least demanding.
questions.hint: Look for the fastest change in the log.

options.misconception: brings an unrelated foundry process into the brief

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish stable patina from active corrosion on bronze.
questions.stem: A conservator describes a bronze as having a hard, even, dark green surface. Which term best fits that surface?

options.text: Surface dirt, because a true patina never appears on a cast bronze
options.misconception: denies that a cast bronze can ever patinate

options.text: Active powdering, because a green surface is always still eating into the bronze
options.misconception: treats any green colour as active corrosion

options.text: A stable patina, which has hardened and no longer corrodes the metal beneath
An applied coating, because real corrosion layers are always evenly coloured
options.misconception: confuses an even layer with an applied coating

questions.explanation: A hard, even, dark green surface that no longer moves is a stable patina, a protective layer formed by the bronze itself. Active powdering is friable and continues to lose metal, and neither dirt nor an applied coating behaves this way.

questions.learningObjective: Plan a carving around a weakness recorded in the outcrop.

questions.stem: Given the quarry report above, which plan best handles the weakness in the outcrop?

options.text: Ignore the fissure, since fissures close up once the block is freed from the bed
options.misconception: believes the natural cleft will seal itself

options.text: Carve the fissure over so that it becomes part of the drapery and hides the weakness
options.misconception: treats a structural flaw as a purely visual matter

options.text: Fill the fissure with a modern mortar so the block becomes structurally continuous
options.misconception: proposes a modern repair inside ancient stone

options.text: Redesign the figure so the fissure falls between the legs and the loose wedge stays outside

questions.explanation: A fissure and a loose wedge dictate the design, so the sculptor must draw the figure around them rather than against them. Hiding a weakness in drapery leaves a structural risk in place, and neither mortar nor self-closing fissures are real options.
questions.hint: The design must fit the stone as it is.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why the design is judged against the block and not the quarry face.

answer.exemplar: The block is the material the sculptor actually has, and every mark on it must be made while the stone is portable and can still be turned. The quarry face shows where the stone happens to lie, with bedding, fissures and old working marks that belong to geology and extraction, not to the sculpture. Judging the design against the face would ignore the cuts already made and the limits they impose.

questions.explanation: The block is what the sculptor works on, and its existing cuts and bedding constrain the design, while the quarry face only records where the stone lay. Judging against the face would ignore the extraction marks the block already carries.
questions.hint: Focus on the piece the sculptor actually holds.

options.misconception: reads a partial loss as no loss

options.misconception: assigns the fault to the very layer being added

options.misconception: blames the size alone for a ground failure

options.text: Add a fresh chalk ground over a sized surface so the new paint sits on top of the grain
Thicken the panel with a support, because a chalk ground can never hold paint
options.misconception: proposes a structural fix for a preparation problem

questions.stem: A joinery note records that a solid oak panel grows in width across the grain as the air becomes damp. Which statement explains this?

options.text: Wood does not move at all, so any change is caused by the paint and its ground
options.misconception: denies that timber responds to humidity

options.text: Wood swells equally in all directions, so the panel grows equally in width and thickness
options.misconception: assumes timber swells isotropically like a liquid

options.text: Wood shrinks when damp because the cell walls absorb less water than the cavities
options.misconception: reverses the direction of moisture response

options.text: Wood changes dimension unevenly with moisture, swelling across the grain and little along it

questions.explanation: Timber expands across the grain as it takes up moisture and changes very little along the grain, which is why a panel in a rigid frame splits across its fibres. Equal swelling in all directions would not produce that failure pattern.

The back press marks the back of the model, which the founder uses to judge the mould

options.misconception: believes the sheet is bonded down by pressing

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how working in situ changes the carving process.
questions.stem: A brief proposes carving a relief panel into the living face of a quarry cliff. Explain why the method of work differs from carving a relief on a detached block.

answer.exemplar: On the cliff face the carver works standing on ladders at height, with no block to turn over and no bench to lay tools on, so the strokes must be planned to be reached from one position. Weather, seepage and the uneven rock surface act directly on the work as it is exposed, and mistakes cannot be corrected by turning the piece over. The composition must also read from the ground below, which limits where figures can be placed.

questions.explanation: On the cliff face the carver cannot turn the work or set up a bench, and the weather acts on the exposed surface at once, so strokes and composition must be planned for that fixed position. A detached block can be turned and protected.
questions.hint: Compare the freedom of turning a block over.

options.misconception: puts the veined cut before the flat one

options.text: Flat chisel, then claw chisel, then tooth chisel, then a polish
options.misconception: swaps the first two tool stages

options.text: Claw chisel, then flat chisel, then tooth chisel, then a polish
Polish, then flat chisel, then claw chisel, then a tooth chisel
options.misconception: reverses the working order of the stages

questions.explanation: Broad channels come first because the claw chisel clears waste, the flat chisel then levels the surface, the tooth chisel cuts the narrow veined detail, and only a polished sheen can follow. Working backwards would mean finishing before the form existed.

options.misconception: claims glue bleach the chalk

options.misconception: attributes the sizing to the wrong layer

It makes the panel surface rough so that the brush will hold more paint
options.misconception: confuses sizing with a textured ground

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how direct carving differs from modelling as a working method.
questions.stem: On a studio visit a client asks how carving differs from modelling, given that both can produce a finished figure. Write the explanation.

answer.exemplar: In carving the artist works by removing material from a solid block, so every decision is a commitment: the form is discovered as the stone comes away and each mark is irreversible. In modelling the artist adds material to a soft substance, so a form can be built, altered and corrected as easily as it is made. The two methods therefore produce different surfaces and different relationships between the maker and the work.

questions.explanation: Carving commits the artist to irreversible decisions as the stone is removed, while modelling allows a form to be built and corrected at will. That difference accounts for the different surfaces and rhythms of the two practices.
questions.hint: Compare removal of material with addition of it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a stable patina is valued on a bronze.
questions.stem: A museum wants to display a bronze that already carries a hard, dark green patina. Explain why this surface is usually preferred to a bright, freshly cleaned metal surface.

answer.exemplar: The hard green patina is the bronze's own corrosion layer, grown slowly and already hardened, and it slows further attack by sealing the metal from moisture and air. A freshly cleaned surface is raw metal that will immediately begin to discolour and dull again, so it would need repeated intervention to stay presentable. The patina therefore records the object's history and reduces the work of maintaining it.

questions.explanation: A hard patina is the bronze's own stable corrosion layer and shields the metal from moisture and air, so it slows further decay. A bright cleaned surface is raw metal that will dull and spot again quickly and would need constant retouching.

questions.stem: Given the sculptor's log above, why does allowing the wrist to travel with the blow improve the carving?

options.text: A travelling wrist strikes the mallet a greater number of times in each minute
options.misconception: suggests the change is about speed of work

A travelling wrist lets the tool stay sharper because it meets the stone more squarely

questions.explanation: Letting the wrist travel with the blow curves the path of the tool around the edge and keeps the impact controlled, which is what the sculptor reports. Nothing about the number of blows, the sharpness of the edge or the mallet's weight changes.
questions.hint: Consider the path of the tool through the stroke.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The chalk ground on a panel
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a chalk ground must be applied over a sized panel.
questions.stem: A conservator must prepare a wooden panel for painting and notices that the previous ground was applied straight to unsized wood. Explain what went wrong and why.

answer.exemplar: Wood is porous and drinks the oil and moisture out of any ground applied directly to it, so the binder is pulled away from the chalk and the layer crumbles or cracks as it dries. Sizing with a thin glue seals the surface and stops that suction, allowing the ground to bind properly and to stay pale and even. The order matters, because a ground laid on raw wood cannot be rescued by later sealing.

questions.explanation: Unsealed wood sucks the binder out of the ground, leaving it weak, uneven and prone to flaking, and a later coat cannot restore what the wood has already absorbed. Sizing first seals the timber so the ground can bind as intended.
questions.hint: Think about how thirsty the bare wood is.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Compute the percentage of a time budget spent on a task.
questions.stem: A workshop allocates 30 hours to direct carving. The first 6 hours go to layout and the rest to removing material. What percentage of the hours are spent removing material?
questions.explanation: Removing material takes 30 minus 6, which is 24 hours, and 24 out of 30 is 0 point 8, which is 80 percent. Counting the layout hours as carving time, or dividing by the layout hours alone, misreports the split.
questions.hint: Subtract the layout hours, then divide by 30.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret measured corrosion to calculate a percentage loss of dimension.
questions.stem: A conservation survey records that a bronze bowl measured 20.0 centimetres across when new and 19.7 centimetres across today. What percentage of the original diameter has been lost?

options.text: 0.3 percent, because the loss of 0.3 is read straight off as a percentage
options.misconception: reads the measurement difference as a percentage

options.text: 1.52 percent, because the loss should be measured against the current diameter
options.misconception: divides by the present diameter instead

options.text: 1.5 percent, because 0.3 divided by 20 gives 0.015
15 percent, because a loss of three tenths is read as three tenths of ten
options.misconception: shifts the decimal point when converting to a percentage

questions.explanation: The bowl has lost 0.3 centimetres of its original 20, and 0.3 divided by 20 is 0.015, which is 1.5 percent. Dividing by today's diameter, reading the raw difference as a percentage, or shifting the decimal each give a different wrong figure.
questions.hint: Divide the loss by the original diameter.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a carving plan against the constraints of the outcrop.
questions.stem: First, the quarry offers a face with a sound lower section and a weathered upper section 2 metres high. Second, the sculptor must place a 3 metre figure. Which plan is best?

options.text: Cut the weathered section away entirely and restore the sound stone with a facing course
options.misconception: proposes a modern facing in place of the old surface

options.text: Carve only the sound lower section and reduce the figure to fit beneath the weathering
options.misconception: abandons the commission instead of reading the stone

options.text: Carve only the weathered upper section, where the soft stone allows finer detail quickly
options.misconception: prefers the layer that will erode first

options.text: Carve the figure across both sections, letting the weathered part supply the drapery texture

questions.explanation: A weathered upper zone is not a liability but a resource: it supplies a ready texture for drapery, so the figure can cross both zones and let the stone's own condition shape part of the design. Replacing it with a modern facing or abandoning the commission both destroy the setting.
questions.hint: Ask whether the weathering can be used rather than removed.
